title: Thermal-plex: fluidic-free, rapid sequential multiplexed imaging with DNA-encoded thermal channels
abstract: Multiplexed fluorescence imaging is typically limited to three- to five-plex on standard setups. Sequential imaging methods based on iterative labeling and imaging enable practical higher multiplexing, but generally require a complex fluidic setup with several rounds of slow buffer exchange (tens of minutes to an hour for each exchange step). We report the thermal-plex method, which removes complex and slow buffer exchange steps and provides fluidic-free, rapid sequential imaging. Thermal-plex uses simple DNA probes that are engineered to fluoresce sequentially when, and only when, activated with transient exposure to heating spikes at designated temperatures (thermal channels). Channel switching is fast (<30 s) and is achieved with a commercially available and affordable on-scope heating device. We demonstrate 15-plex RNA imaging (five thermal × three fluorescence channels) in fixed cells and retina tissues in less than 4 min, without using buffer exchange or fluidics. Thermal-plex introduces a new labeling method for efficient sequential multiplexed imaging.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Thermal-plex shows clear scholarly uptake: it has 18 OpenAlex citations, places in the top 10% of papers in its field and year, and has 19 documented downstream reuses. Its citation trail is concentrated in high-visibility venues across fluorescence imaging, chemical sensing, and molecular engineering, suggesting that the method is already being used as a reference point for related multiplexed imaging approaches.

Full narrative

Published in Nature Methods in 2023, Thermal-plex addresses a practical bottleneck in sequential multiplexed fluorescence imaging: the slow and complex buffer-exchange steps required by fluidic systems. By introducing DNA-encoded thermal channels, the paper proposes a fluidic-free approach intended to speed sequential imaging while simplifying experimental setup. That technical framing aligns closely with the article’s citation footprint, which is concentrated in adjacent areas such as advanced biosensing, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, and advanced fluorescence microscopy techniques.

The article’s impact is already visible in both citations and reuse. OpenAlex records 18 citations, and the paper is classified in the top 10% most-cited for its field and publication year. Beyond direct citations, there are 19 documented downstream reuses, including articles, preprints, a conference paper, and a review. This pattern suggests that Thermal-plex is being taken up not only as a result to cite, but also as a methodological template for follow-on work.

The citing landscape points to active cross-pollination across the multiplex imaging and DNA-encoded sensing space. Recent citing works include studies in Nature Biotechnology, Nature Communications, Analytical Chemistry, Advanced Science, and Journal of the American Chemical Society, as well as multiple bioRxiv preprints. Several of these newer papers focus on rapid sequential imaging, DNA strand displacement, fluorescence barcoding, or signal-exchange strategies, indicating that Thermal-plex is part of an evolving toolkit for higher-plex imaging and detection workflows.

Stewardship signals are also strong. The article is linked to a GitHub repository and a Zenodo record, and the digest reports dataset citation handling as successful. Those artifacts improve the work’s reproducibility and make it easier for other groups to adapt the method. Funding from major biomedical and research organizations, together with the Harvard and Howard Hughes Medical Institute affiliations of the author group, further situates the paper within a well-supported research program in imaging and DNA nanotechnology.

Overall, the record shows an early but substantive influence profile: a methods paper with clear technical relevance, rapid citation uptake, and evidence of reuse across closely related fields. The available data support a conclusion of growing methodological importance, especially for researchers developing faster and less infrastructure-intensive multiplex imaging platforms.
